doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: Tape editing with Billy Taylor and Turtle Island String Quartet
summary: He recalls a daring grease-pencil tape cut on a 24-track session with Billy Taylor, and discusses splicing blocks.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I assume that you’ve taken a razor blade to tape a number of times?

I have. I remember doing a project with Dr. Billy Taylor and the Turtle Island String Quartet and it was 24-track analog, one of the last projects I guess I did on 24-track analog. And he was doing some sort of I guess best could be called a cadenza and it came down and there was this downbeat and then we were going to cut to something else. And you know sometimes when you rock tape you can hear what you need to do rather easily. And there was one thing, I don’t know, and I even — the tape was rolling and just at the spot I just tapped the tape as it was going just to see if I could then hear and see where I thought the spot was. Tapped it with a grease pencil. And it was like all right, you know, I made the cut, put it together, and it played back and we were like, “Wait, let’s play that again.” I played it again and Dr. Taylor just turned to me with his big glasses and he went, “That shouldn’t have worked.” But it did you know. But I used to love that sort of stuff. I was fearless about editing tape.

I remember the first time I saw it happen I was astounded actually. And then to learn that it happens in classical performances also, I guess I didn’t envision that it would even be used in the classical world.
